#datetime (package jsdate): the JavaScript engine's Date

On this page

  • The time zone callback
  • Using it
  • How we know it is correct
  • Integration

src/engine/datetime is the ECMAScript Date calendar and string handling, written natively in Odin (the package is named jsdate so it never collides with core:time/datetime). It is ported from QuickJS-ng and produces the same results as QuickJS over the whole valid range, so Date behaves identically without the C that used to run in WebAssembly.

Time values are milliseconds since the Unix epoch as f64, NaN for an invalid Date; the valid range is ±8.64 × 10¹⁵ ms (about ±273 790 years). Fields use the ECMAScript order [year, month(0–11), day(1–31), hour, min, sec, ms, weekday, tz-minutes].

The package is allocation-free and has no OS dependency, so it builds for windows_amd64, linux_amd64 and freestanding_wasm32. The one thing it cannot compute on its own — the local time zone offset — is a host callback.

#The time zone callback

Odin
import jsdate "wb:engine/datetime"

jsdate.timezone_offset_proc = proc "contextless" (time_ms: i64) -> int {
    return host_get_timezone_offset(time_ms) // minutes west of UTC, i.e. getTimezoneOffset(t)
}

This is the exact role of js.timezone_offset in the Wren host. When the callback is nil, local time equals UTC, so UTC-only code (and tests) work with no host wired up.

#Using it

Odin
// time value -> fields (UTC or local)
f, ok := jsdate.get_date_fields(t_ms, is_local = true, force = false)
// fields -> time value (MakeDay/MakeTime/MakeDate + TimeClip, with month/day overflow)
t := jsdate.set_date_fields(f, is_local = true)

// formatting
buf: [64]u8
n := jsdate.format_date(buf[:], f, .ISO,     .All)  // 2018-01-02T23:02:56.927Z
n  = jsdate.format_date(buf[:], f, .UTC,     .All)  // Tue, 02 Jan 2018 23:04:46 GMT
n  = jsdate.format_date(buf[:], f, .ToString,.All)  // Wed Jan 03 2018 00:05:22 GMT+0100
n  = jsdate.format_date(buf[:], f, .Locale,  .All)  // 1/2/2018, 11:40:40 PM

// parsing (Date.parse / new Date(string))
t = jsdate.parse("2018-01-02T23:02:56.927Z")        // strict ISO 8601
t = jsdate.parse("Wed Jan 03 2018 00:05:22 GMT+0100") // legacy browser format

get_date_fields returns ok = false for a NaN time when force is false (the caller then emits "Invalid Date", or a RangeError for toISOString). set_date_fields performs the spec's MakeDay / MakeTime / MakeDate in f64 with the operation order ECMAScript mandates, so out-of-range months and days roll over exactly as required (and the fp-evaluation-order test262 case passes).

parse tries the strict ISO form first, then the legacy "other" format: weekday and month abbreviations, GMT±HHMM, named zones (GMT, UTC, PST, CET, …), AM/PM, parenthesized comments, and the loose day/month/year ordering old browsers accept. Input is folded to ASCII first (U+2212 → -, anything else above 255 → x) and capped at 127 bytes, matching QuickJS.

#How we know it is correct

A differential judge compiles QuickJS's Date calendar and parser (copied verbatim from quickjs.c) with zig cc, using the same deterministic, instant-dependent time-zone rule on both sides, and compares over 1,500,000+ cases:

  • set_date_fields on random fields, including out-of-range months and days and years spanning ±300 000, in both UTC and local mode;
  • get_date_fields on random time values, the ±8.64e15 limits and NaN, in UTC and local, with and without force;
  • the UTC calendar inverse (set(get(t)) == t) — local time is intentionally non-invertible when the offset varies with the instant, exactly as in QuickJS;
  • parse on ISO and UTC strings generated from random times, plus a battery of hand-written legacy forms and the ±extreme-year ISO boundaries.

Result: 0 mismatches.

#Integration

The engine wires timezone_offset_proc to js.timezone_offset, backs Date objects with the f64 time value, and calls set_date_fields for the Date constructor / Date.UTC / the setters, get_date_fields for the getters, format_date for the toString family, and parse for Date.parse and new Date(string). Date.now and new Date() still read the clock from the host.
